item.title: 5 Signs You Should Sell Your House For Cash Instead of Listing
item.dc:creator: wholesalepro
item.content:encoded:
If you own a house and you are trying to decide whether to list it with an agent or sell it for cash, you are probably getting a lot of conflicting advice. The truth is that a traditional listing makes sense in some situations and a direct cash sale makes sense in others. The right answer depends entirely on your specific circumstances.

1. You Need to Close in Less Than 30 Days

The median time from listing a house to closing on a traditional sale is approximately 65-75 days. If your timeline is shorter — because of a foreclosure deadline, a job relocation, a divorce agreement, or any other urgent situation — a traditional listing cannot deliver. A cash sale can. Most cash buyers close in 7-14 days.

2. Your Property Needs Significant Repairs

Traditional buyers financing with a mortgage cannot purchase properties in rough condition. Their lender will require an appraisal, and major deficiencies will either cause the loan to be declined or require repairs before closing. Cash buyers purchase as-is. No repairs, no preparation, no staging.

3. You Are Behind on Your Mortgage or Property Taxes

If foreclosure proceedings have started, the clock is running. A traditional sale requires 60+ days. In many pre-foreclosure situations, that is not enough time. A cash sale can close in days if necessary — the only option that can reliably beat a foreclosure auction date.

4. The Property Is Vacant or Has Become a Financial Burden

Vacant properties cost money every month: mortgage, insurance, taxes, utilities, maintenance. Every month you hold while pursuing a traditional sale is another month of carrying costs. A fast cash sale eliminates those costs immediately upon closing.

5. You Want a Guaranteed Outcome Without Contingencies

Approximately 15-20% of signed purchase contracts in the United States fail to close. Cash sales remove the financing contingency, the appraisal contingency, and most inspection contingencies. For sellers who cannot afford the risk of a deal falling apart, the certainty of a cash sale has real value that a simple price comparison does not capture.

The Bottom Line

A cash sale is not right for every seller. If your property is in excellent condition, you have no time pressure, and you want to maximize price, a traditional listing will likely net you more money. But for sellers who check one or more of the five boxes above, the value of speed, certainty, and as-is purchase often outweighs the price difference.
item.excerpt:encoded: Wondering whether to list or sell for cash? Here are five specific situations where a direct cash sale is the better financial and practical choice.

item.title: How to Analyze a Wholesale Real Estate Deal in Under 10 Minutes
item.dc:creator: wholesalepro
item.content:encoded:
Every wholesale real estate deal analysis comes down to three numbers and two formulas. Once you understand them, you can evaluate most deals in under ten minutes.

The Three Numbers That Matter

  • After Repair Value (ARV) - What the property will be worth after full renovation.
  • Estimated Repair Cost (ERC) - What it will cost to bring it to retail condition.
  • Purchase Price (PP) - What the wholesaler is asking.

The 70% Rule

The most widely used benchmark in wholesale real estate: Maximum Purchase Price = (ARV x 0.70) minus Repair Cost

Example: ARV $200,000, repairs $40,000. Max offer = ($200,000 x 0.70) - $40,000 = $100,000. The 30% spread covers closing costs, holding costs, selling costs, and profit margin.

How to Find the ARV

Pull comparable sales — properties similar in size, type, condition, and location that sold within the last 90 days. You want fully renovated comparables, not distressed sales. Use MLS access or Zillow recently sold as a starting point.

How to Estimate Repairs

Light cosmetic rehab: $15-$25 per square foot. Moderate rehab including kitchen and bath: $30-$50 per square foot. Full gut renovation: $75-$100+ per square foot. Always verify with a contractor walkthrough before committing.

The Bottom Line

Use the 70% rule as a first filter. If the asking price is at or below your maximum allowable offer, pursue deeper due diligence. If it is significantly above, pass or counter with your number and explain your math.
item.excerpt:encoded: New to wholesale real estate? A simple step-by-step framework for analyzing any deal in under 10 minutes using three numbers and two formulas.

item.title: What Happens to Your Credit Score in a Foreclosure
item.dc:creator: wholesalepro
item.content:encoded:
A foreclosure drops your credit score by 85-160 points and stays on your report for seven years. Understanding exactly what happens — and when — is critical whether you are trying to avoid foreclosure or rebuilding afterward.

How Much Does a Foreclosure Drop Your Credit Score?

The exact drop varies based on your score before the event. A homeowner with a 780 credit score may see it drop to the low 600s — approximately 150 points. A homeowner with a 620 score may see it drop to 530-540. The higher your starting score, the more points you stand to lose.

The Missed Payments Come First

The credit damage actually begins with the first missed payment — long before the foreclosure is completed. A mortgage payment that is 30 days late will typically drop a credit score by 60-110 points. By the time a foreclosure is formally completed, most homeowners have already accumulated 3-6 months of missed payment history.

How Long Does a Foreclosure Stay on Your Credit Report?

Seven years from the date of the first missed payment — not from the date the foreclosure was completed. The practical impact diminishes over time, with the heaviest weight placed on events within the last 24 months.

A Cash Sale Before Foreclosure Preserves Your Credit

The most effective way to protect your credit in a pre-foreclosure situation is to sell the property before the foreclosure is completed. A sale that pays off the mortgage in full typically reports as paid as agreed — even if you made several late payments before the sale. This is the central argument for a cash sale in pre-foreclosure: it is faster, more certain, and preserves your credit outcome.
item.excerpt:encoded: A foreclosure drops your credit score by 85-160 points and stays on your report for 7 years. Learn what happens and how a cash sale can protect you.

item.title: Inherited a House? Do This Before You Make Any Decisions
item.dc:creator: wholesalepro
item.content:encoded:
Inheriting a house brings a complicated mix of emotions and practical decisions arriving at the same time. Before you decide what to do, take these five steps to protect your legal rights, your tax position, and all of your options.

Step 1: Determine How the Property Was Held

In a living trust, the property transfers immediately without probate. With joint tenancy with right of survivorship, it transfers to the surviving co-owner automatically. In the deceased person's name alone, it must go through probate before it can be transferred or sold — a process that varies from 3 months to 18 months depending on the state.

Step 2: Secure and Insure the Property Immediately

Vacant properties are targets for theft and vandalism. Standard homeowner policies exclude coverage for properties vacant more than 30-60 days. Get a vacant property endorsement immediately.

Step 3: Understand the Stepped-Up Basis

When you inherit property, your cost basis for capital gains purposes is stepped up to the fair market value on the date of death. If the deceased paid $60,000 in 1985 and the property is worth $320,000 today, your basis is $320,000. Selling at $320,000 means zero capital gains tax. Consult a tax professional before making any sale decisions.

Step 4: Assess the Property Financial Position

Know the mortgage balance, property tax status, any liens, the estimated market value, and the cost to bring it to marketable condition before committing to any course of action.

Step 5: Consider All Three Options

Keep it, rent it, or sell it. Each has distinct financial and practical implications. Cash buyers can work within the probate timeline and close as soon as the court authorizes the sale — often the simplest path when multiple heirs are involved or the property needs significant repairs.
item.excerpt:encoded: Inheriting a house is complicated. Before you decide what to do, take these five steps to protect your legal rights, tax position, and all of your options.

item.title: The 70 Percent Rule in Wholesale Real Estate — Explained Simply
item.dc:creator: wholesalepro
item.content:encoded:
If you spend any time in wholesale real estate circles, you will hear the 70% rule referenced constantly. New investors treat it as a sacred formula. Experienced investors treat it as a starting point. Here is what it actually is, why it exists, and where it breaks down.

What the 70% Rule Says

Maximum Purchase Price = (ARV x 0.70) minus Estimated Repair Cost. If a property has an ARV of $250,000 and needs $50,000 in repairs, the maximum purchase price is ($250,000 x 0.70) - $50,000 = $125,000.

Why 70%? What Is the Other 30% For?

The 30% covers: closing costs on purchase (1-2%), holding costs (1-2%), financing costs (8-12% annually on hard money), selling costs including commissions (6-8%), and profit margin (10-20% of ARV). Added together, these consume 20-28% of ARV on a typical flip. The remaining 2-10% is margin of safety for surprises.

Where the Rule Works Well

Average price range markets ($100K-$350K ARV) with moderate repair scopes and predictable days-on-market. As a quick filter for screening dozens of deal packages without deep analysis on each one.

Where the Rule Breaks Down

High-ARV markets: On $600K-$1M properties, fixed costs do not scale proportionally. Many investors use 75-80% rules. Low-ARV markets: On $60K-$100K properties, fixed renovation costs consume a larger percentage of ARV. Cosmetic-only flips often support 75-80%.

The Rule Is a Ceiling, Not a Target

The 70% rule gives you the maximum you should pay. Your actual offer should be below that ceiling to allow for renovation surprises. Experienced investors routinely buy at 60-65% of ARV minus repairs. Use the 70% rule to quickly eliminate overpriced deals — not to set your offer price.
item.excerpt:encoded: The 70% rule is the most widely used benchmark in wholesale real estate. A clear explanation of what it is, why it exists, and where it breaks down.
